doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Meeting George Wettling and playing with McPartland and Red Allen
summary: Through Wettling he joined the Condon and McPartland circle, toured with Jimmy McPartland and played with Red Allen.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well tell me how the gig with Louis Armstrong happened for you.

Well a break in the night. I knocked around for a while and you know, you get to know people that are similarly inclined, you know, your kind of jazz. And I got to know George Wettling. There was a guy named Dick Webb, the trombone player, he was the editor of Boating magazine. A very nice trombone player and a darling guy, he was the greatest guy in the world, quite a sailor, I used to do a lot of sailing with him. And Dick knew George Wettling and I lived in the Village and George Wettling lived a block or two away from me. And somehow we met and we hit it off. George was a great guy, he was wonderful. He got drunk, and I heard he got nasty, but he never did that with me. He never had any kids and I was like a son. And I liked the music. And so he got me together with Condon and Wild Bill and that group, and McPartland. He was a very good friend of Jimmy McPartland. So I got to play with Jimmy McPartland and got on the scene, and Jimmy, and Marian is still around, a wonderful gal. And I think the first time I made

more than $100, it was $150, was with Jimmy McPartland and we had to drive to Cleveland and back. And I went on the road with him too. And the Dixieland and that old tradition, that old time Chicago jazz, it continued in Ohio in Columbus and Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, and places like that, they had clubs and the people were still interested in that kind of music. So I got all involved in that and things went along and went along. I played with this one and that one and there was a guy named Max Amayer, a booking agent sort of. And he called me a couple of times, three or four times, to play with Red Allen which was a wonderful experience. Red was a marvelous guy. I mean Red was up there with Louis Armstrong. Red Allen was just a natural — you listen to those old records. You get tired of playing Louis all the time. A little refreshing change is Red Allen. So I played with Red and then there was a scene called Stuyvesant Casino where Bunk Johnson came. That was the first live jazz band almost that I saw, certainly the first black New Orleans band. Bunk Johnson at the Stuyvesant. I was there opening night. As a matter of fact there are some photographs. I saw them in Japan in some magazine about Bunk Johnson’s opening night and there I am.
